title: Texts in which learners see themselves
statement: Choose texts whose names, characters and cultures let learners see themselves, since culturally familiar material is read faster, recalled more accurately and understood with fewer errors.
detail: The reading course plans' digest of a national reading report records that students reading culturally familiar material read it faster, recalled it more accurately and made fewer comprehension errors than with unfamiliar material, and draws the reverse risk for tests: assessments built on culturally narrow content disadvantage students unfamiliar with it. A teaching move in a Grade 3 reading red-team standard, drawn from a regional education laboratory video, makes identity-affirming selection a text-quality criterion, choosing texts whose content, names and characters can affirm the learner's identity, culture and language. The evidence is a cited report and a video, not a measurement in these courses.
against: The record no-local-knowledge-the-course-doesnt-teach keeps items solvable without local or cultural knowledge the course doesn't teach, in neutral settings; that limits what an item may require rather than which texts are chosen, but the digest's own note warns that content familiar to one group is unfamiliar to another.

evidence.quote: Students reading culturally familiar material read it faster, recalled it more accurately, and made fewer comprehension errors than when reading unfamiliar material.
